# The H100 got more expensive

Compute is getting pricier, not cheaper. Here is what that does to debt, power and sites.

Jose Mir

Oct 27, 2026

Issue 1 · Tuesday, October 27, 2026 · 5-minute read

Welcome to THREE PHASE. AI infrastructure moves in three phases: Capital decides what gets funded, Build decides what gets powered and built, and Compute decides who actually uses it. Most coverage picks one lane. The interesting moves happen where the lanes touch, so every Tuesday we read all three together, early and without an agenda.

A three-year-old chip is earning more rent than it did a year ago. If compute were in oversupply, H100 prices would be falling. They are not, and that changes the math for lenders, builders and buyers at once.

### One Big Thing · Phase 3 · Compute

What happened: Nebius raised on-demand GPU prices on October 1, its second hike in about three months. Independent trackers show the same direction across the market.

Why it matters: The bear case on AI infrastructure assumed GPUs lose value fast. Rental rates are the cleanest test of that assumption, and so far the test is failing.

By the numbers:

- Nebius list price for an H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour; B300 from $7.85 to $9.50.
- The Ornn H100 index settled at $3.17 on October 23, up about 4% in a month.

Our read: This is a Compute story with a Capital ending. GPU-backed loans were underwritten on falling collateral values. If older chips keep earning, useful lives stretch and those loans look better than feared. The constraint is moving to power and memory: a Dell executive told an audience he sees about 20% more memory supply next year against roughly 200% more demand. Capacity that is already powered and running is the scarce asset, not the chip itself.

The question: If a 2023 GPU rents for more today than in 2025, what depreciation schedule should a lender actually use?

### Phase 1 · Capital

$105 billion, rated. S&P Global Ratings published a dashboard of 32 North American data centre deals carrying $105.3 billion of debt, backed by 8.7 GW. Project finance is 58% of the dollars.

So what: Lenders are underwriting individual projects, which means power and lease terms get read line by line.

CBRE buys inside the walls. CBRE agreed to buy Onnec for $610 million in cash, plus up to $400 million in earnouts. Onnec installs equipment inside hyperscale halls.

So what: The fees are migrating from the building to what goes in it, and brokers are following them.

### Phase 2 · Build

Google buys flexibility, at gigawatt scale. Google and Voltus expanded their PJM virtual power plant to about 1 GW of batteries, thermostats and load shifting. Two weeks earlier, FERC rejected most of PJM's interim large-load plan.

So what: When market design stalls, the biggest buyers bring their own capacity rather than wait for the rules.

Behind-the-meter fills to 2028. Calgary-based Enerflex booked over 1 GW of on-site gas generation for an unnamed data centre. Its behind-the-meter backlog now tops 1.75 GW.

So what: Factory slots for on-site power are being claimed in gigawatt blocks. Smaller projects queue behind them.

### Phase 3 · Compute

A frontier lab picks Nova Scotia. Anthropic signed its first Canadian data centre lease with EverWind at Point Tupper, part of a planned C$10 billion-plus campus paired with wind.

So what: Demand is going where land, power and a buildable plan already line up, even far from the usual hubs.

Open models take the tokens. A Dell executive claims about 80% of tokens are now generated by open models, driven by cost, with inference spreading to the edge.

So what: One vendor's number, but if it holds, inference demand spreads across more sites, at smaller sizes.

### The Chart · Gas turbines on order

Sources: GE Vernova, Utility Dive

GE Vernova's gas turbine backlog plus slot reservations went from 55 GW in mid-2025 to 116 GW by mid-2026. The next print lands October 28.

Takeaway: More than doubled in a year. Turbine supply is now a schedule, not a purchase.

### By Seat

If you allocate capital… firm rental rates help GPU collateral; check which leases sit behind it.

If you develop or own land… energized capacity is outrunning new capacity on value. Time to power is the whole story.

If you supply energy or compute… buyers are paying for flexibility and on-site supply, not just megawatt-hours.

### Question of the Week

Is the rising price of older GPUs a sign of real scarcity, or of a market that has not yet seen the next generation land in volume?

What are you seeing? Hit reply. We read every one.
